analysis.one_liner: Requires drug makers to sell medicines for Medicare patients at no more than the prices they charge abroad.
analysis.headline: The bill, which its backers said would cut seniors' drug prices by about 40%, never received a hearing or a vote and died in committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced companies that sell prescription drugs to the federal government to also sell them to pharmacies, in quantities matching what Medicare beneficiaries buy, at a price no higher than the average price the company charges in six other countries including Canada, Germany, and Japan. Seniors paying cash at the pharmacy often pay far more than foreign buyers and than big insurers, so the bill aimed to close that gap without new government spending. It was referred to two House committees in March 2003, sent to a health subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who buy prescription drugs out of pocket. The bill's findings state that older Americans often pay twice as much as consumers abroad — in some cases ten times as much — and estimate that its approach would cut brand-name drug prices for many beneficiaries by about 40%. Pharmacies would also gain, because they could buy the drugs they dispense to Medicare patients at the lower price rather than paying high wholesale prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors on Medicare buying prescription drugs

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires each manufacturer that sells drugs to the U.S. government to make the same drugs available to pharmacies, in amounts equal to what those pharmacies dispense to Medicare beneficiaries, at a price no greater than the manufacturer's average foreign price.

The bill's findings state that older Americans often pay twice as much for prescription drugs as consumers in foreign nations and the manufacturers' most favored U.S. customers, and in some cases ten times as much, and estimate the policy would reduce prices for many Medicare beneficiaries by an average of 40 percent.
The bill extends the same lower prices to drugs furnished through Medicare-certified hospice programs, aimed at terminally ill patients.

Manufacturers that fail to comply would be debarred — excluded from government contracting for a period commensurate with the violation — giving the rule an enforcement tool without new federal spending.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose profits from U.S. sales would shrink as prices for drugs sold to Medicare beneficiaries were pulled down to levels in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the United Kingdom. The bill's own findings acknowledge this would reduce industry profits that it cites at $27.3 billion in 1999. There is no federal spending involved; the cost falls on manufacturers' margins.

drawbacks.text: Economists and the industry would argue that pegging U.S. prices to foreign government-negotiated prices could reduce revenue that funds research into new medicines, slowing the development of future drugs.

A design weakness is built in: the bill only applies to a 'participating manufacturer' — one that enters a contract with the United States to sell drugs. A company could avoid the price requirement by not contracting directly with the federal government, so the enforcement mechanism may not reach all drug makers.

Because the benchmark is an average of prices in other countries, manufacturers would have an incentive to raise prices abroad or press foreign governments for higher prices in order to raise the U.S. benchmark, which would shift some cost pressure onto consumers in those countries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a direct, no-new-spending way to cut what seniors pay at the pharmacy by linking U.S. prices to the prices Americans' own tax dollars and purchasing power already obtain elsewhere. Its honest weaknesses are the contracting loophole in its own definition, and the long-run tradeoff that lower drug revenue may mean slower development of new medicines. For current Medicare beneficiaries facing prices two to ten times higher than foreign buyers pay, the immediate benefit is concrete and large; the innovation cost is real but uncertain and deferred.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and then to a health subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Allen of Maine introduced the Prescription Drug Fairness for Seniors Act on March 20, 2003, with 29 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, the two panels with jurisdiction over prescription drug policy.

Within days it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and it never advanced past that subcommittee; no hearing, markup, or vote on the bill appears anywhere in its action history.
The bill ultimately drew 58 cosponsors — 57 Democrats and 1 Independent — and no Republicans, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2005 with the bill still stalled in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: the bill died without a vote, so they continued to charge Medicare beneficiaries U.S. prices well above what they charge in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the United Kingdom. Seniors who buy their own medicines gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Tom Allen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the House floor in June 2003.

for.name: 57 of 205 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Sherrod Brown, Henry Waxman, and John Conyers.

against.name: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Chair of the primary committee of referral
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 20, 2003 and never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or committee vote; the bill was sent to the Health Subcommittee on March 26 and stayed there.

against.name: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Chair of the second committee of referral
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 20, 2003 and took no recorded action on the bill.

against.name: Pharmaceutical research and manufacturing industry
against.what_they_did: The industry publicly campaigned against foreign price-reference and price-control proposals during the 108th Congress, as Congress instead moved toward the Medicare Modernization Act, which barred the government from negotiating drug prices.

sides.party_line_note: All 58 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's one Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and with Republicans controlling the House, the bill never left committee.

industries.note: The bill would cap the price at which participating manufacturers sell drugs used by Medicare beneficiaries at their average foreign price — levels the bill's findings say are roughly half what U.S. seniors pay. Manufacturers would bear the cost directly through reduced margins on U.S. sales.

Pharmacies could purchase drugs for Medicare beneficiaries at the capped foreign-reference price instead of paying high wholesale prices, improving their economics on prescriptions dispensed to seniors.
Drugs furnished to Medicare beneficiaries in hospice care would count toward the purchase amounts pharmacies can buy at the reduced price, extending the price relief to terminally ill patients.
